summary: Defines a minimal set of requirements that an instant messaging and presence protocol must meet. This is an informational memo.

plainLanguage.summary: Before building a chat system, this lists the things it must do at the very least.

questions: what is polite blocking in presence
presence and instant messaging security requirements
subtitle: The minimum checklist that any standard instant messaging and presence protocol had to satisfy.

tldr.problem: Instant messaging and presence applications used independent, non-standard and non-interoperable vendor protocols, so independently built applications could not work together.
tldr.mechanism: The IMPP Working Group lists the minimal requirements a standard protocol MUST or SHOULD meet: naming and scale, access control, intermediaries, encryption, common formats, delivery behavior and detailed security rules.
tldr.outcome: The memo is a requirements list, not a protocol. It sets the yardstick against which proposed IMPP protocols would be judged.

facts.label: Scale goal
facts.value: Millions of entities per domain and millions of domains

today: RFC 2779 is an Informational memo, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It states requirements only and does not define a protocol.

sections.title: Goal and Terminology
sections.content:
Presence is a way to find, retrieve and subscribe to changes in the presence information (such as online or offline) of other users. Instant messaging is a way to send small, simple messages that are delivered immediately to online users. The goal of the IMPP Working Group is a standard protocol so that independently developed applications can interoperate across the Internet.

The terms of the model are taken from RFC 2778, including presentity, watcher, subscriber, notification and instant inbox. The memo adds a few terms of its own, such as administrator, domain, firewall and identifier.

MUST and SHOULD are used in a special sense here: MUST means a proposed solution has to meet the requirement, SHOULD means it may choose not to. The RFC notes this differs from RFC 2119.
sections.plainLanguage: It says what the chat system is for and gives names to all the parts, so everyone talks about the same things. MUST means you have to do it, and SHOULD means you probably will.

sections.title: Requirements Shared by Presence and Messaging
sections.content:
The protocols must suit mobile wireless devices, with high latency, low bandwidth, intermittent connectivity, modest computing power and small displays, and must be reasonably efficient for small payloads.

Names and scale. A presence service must be usable without an instant message service, and the other way around. Each domain must manage its own entities independently, and any number of domains must be allowed. Entities in different domains must interoperate without having known each other before. The design goals include millions of entities in one domain, millions of domains, subscribers with hundreds of subscriptions and presentities with hundreds of subscribers.

Access control. The principal behind a presentity must control who can watch it, who can subscribe, what each watcher sees and who can update it. The principal behind an instant inbox must control who can send to it and who can read from it. Access control must work even when the presentity is out of contact.

Topology and security. Subscriptions, notifications and messages must work both directly and through intermediaries such as proxies, and administrators must be able to allow or block the protocol through common firewalls. Messages must be protectable against corruption, tampering, replay and unwanted reading, but clients must not be forced to use these protections at all times.
sections.plainLanguage: The system has to work on small phones, grow to millions of people, and let each person decide who can see them or message them. It must also work with go-betweens and keep messages private and untampered.

sections.title: Requirements for Presence Information
sections.content:
All entities must produce and consume at least a common base presence format. It must identify the presentity, carry contact information such as email address or telephone number, and be extensible without breaking the base fields. The format SHOULD be based on IETF standards such as vCard (RFC 2426) if possible.

A fetcher must be able to fetch presence information, and a subscriber must be able to subscribe, even when the presentity is out of contact. When information changes, the service MUST notify each subscriber unless access rules prevent it. The protocol must detect when a presentity or subscriber has gone out of contact and must not rely on it saying goodbye, since failures can be unplanned.

Caching of presence information must be possible, and cached copies must be updated when the master changes, without bypassing access rules or limiting the choice of authentication and encryption. Notification must be rapid, which is met if it travels as fast as an instant message would.
sections.plainLanguage: Everybody must describe whether they are around in the same way. The system has to keep working when someone's phone dies suddenly, and tell friends quickly when your status changes.

sections.title: Requirements for Instant Messages
sections.content:
All entities that send or receive instant messages must implement at least a common base message format. It MUST identify the sender and intended recipient and include a return address for replies. It SHOULD include other contact means such as telephone numbers or email addresses, and SHOULD be based on MIME (RFC 2045). It must allow the payload to be encoded and identified so that non-ASCII or encrypted content is possible.

The protocol must reflect best current practice for internationalization and accessibility. The sender MUST be able to learn of successful delivery or the reasons for failure. Transport must be fast enough for comfortable conversational exchanges of short messages.

In a system that supports both services, the common presence format must define a minimum presence schema and be able to represent the status conditions OPEN and CLOSED.
sections.plainLanguage: Every message has to say who sent it and who it is for, and let the receiver reply. The sender should find out if it was delivered, and chat must feel quick.

sections.title: Security Requirements
sections.content:
The security rules were derived from a set of broad security expectations, which the appendix describes. They are written as a subscriber A and a presentity owner B. For subscriptions, A must be able to authenticate that the presentity is controlled by B, and B must be able to identify and authenticate A, refuse or cancel any subscription, and block anonymous principals. No third party may force A to subscribe or cancel A's subscription. B may also use "polite blocking": denying a subscription while it appears granted. Neither side may be required to reveal its IP address to the other.

For notifications, only the intended recipient may read them, receivers must be able to verify the sender and accuracy, and spoofing must be prevented. For instant messages, the sender MUST receive confirmation of non-delivery, the recipient MUST get a delivered message only once, content must be protected from viewing and tampering, the recipient must be able to verify the sender, and the protocol MUST allow signing using existing digital signature standards.

Administrators may hold privileges beyond those of principals, and implementations must handle that without breaking the requirements placed on principals.
sections.plainLanguage: You choose who may follow your status and message you, and nobody can fake being you or read your mail. You can even quietly ignore someone without telling them.
